title: Auto-ARGUE: LLM-Based Report Generation Evaluation
research_question: Can the ARGUE framework for evaluating long-form citation-backed reports be automated with an LLM judge while retaining useful agreement with human judgments of coverage and citation support?
methodology: Auto-ARGUE implements ARGUE as a sequence of sentence-level binary judgments, using few-shot LLM judging for non-trivial decisions and deterministic lookup where possible. It evaluates report content through question-answer nuggets, including AND and OR structures, and separately assesses citation relevance, citation support, repeated information, and assertions of ignorance. Report-level metrics include sentence precision, nugget recall, weighted variants, F1, and finer-grained citation measures. The authors validate the implementation on 51 TREC 2024 NeuCLIR runs across Chinese, Russian, and Farsi collections and on assessor-judged TREC 2024 RAG AG and RAG runs.

key_findings.finding: Auto-ARGUE produced system-level rankings that agreed well with human ARGUE judgments on the TREC NeuCLIR report-generation pilot, with especially strong agreement for sentence precision.

On TREC RAG 2024, Auto-ARGUE nugget recall correlated moderately to strongly with AutoNuggetizer's human-grounded nugget-support evaluation, with Spearman correlations of 0.81-0.86 and Kendall correlations of 0.65-0.72.
The framework directly operationalizes evidence completeness as nugget recall rather than treating factual correctness alone as sufficient report quality.
ARGUE explicitly represents justified abstention-like behavior through negative assertions, rewarding claims of unavailable information only when the corresponding nugget truly has no answer.
The paper's NeuCLIR validation did not test negative-assertion judgments because every NeuCLIR nugget was answerable.
Fine-grained inspection with ARGUE-viz revealed that the authors' own NeuCLIR systems repeatedly struggled with AND nuggets requiring multiple answers.
Citation scoring requires each cited document to support the entire sentence that cites it, which creates a structural preference for simpler sentences.

limitations: The main validation is system-level ranking agreement, so the reported results do not establish equally strong reliability for every individual sentence, nugget, or report.
The NeuCLIR experiments cannot validate the negative-assertion or justified-ignorance branch because all evaluated nuggets were answerable.
The requirement that every cited document support an entire citing sentence can disadvantage complex sentences whose claims are jointly supported by multiple sources.
Evaluation quality depends on the chosen LLM judge, prompts, nugget construction, relevance labels, and document-to-nugget mappings.
The empirical study is restricted to TREC 2024 tasks and does not directly test temporal drift, stale evidence, changing source versions, or distribution shift over time.
The RAG comparison converts AutoNuggetizer claims into question-answer nuggets with an LLM, adding an additional transformation step to the comparison.
raw_claims: Auto-ARGUE automates the binary sentence-level decisions required by the ARGUE report-evaluation framework.
Nugget recall measures how much of the expected information a report correctly covers.
Sentence precision measures whether sentences requiring evidence are fully supported by their citations.
Negative assertions are rewarded only when the relevant information is genuinely absent from the reference nuggets.
NeuCLIR evaluation covered 51 runs over 21 topics for each of three source languages.
All NeuCLIR nuggets in the experiment were answerable, so negative-assertion judgments were not exercised.
The TREC RAG comparison produced Spearman correlations between 0.81 and 0.86 and Kendall correlations between 0.65 and 0.72.
Auto-ARGUE and ARGUE-viz are released as open-source tools.
